title: Genomic analysis of early case samples from the 2025 Marburg virus outbreak in Ethiopia.
abstract: In November 2025, Ethiopia reported its first outbreak of Marburg virus disease, with a case fatality rate of 64%. Here we report the analysis of seven near-complete Marburg virus genomes from seven early cases. The outbreak lineage belonged to the MARV.A.1 clade, which is closely related to genomes from historical human cases and bats. A high nucleotide identity across the seven genomes suggests human-to-human transmission after a zoonotic spillover event. These findings highlight the importance of genomic surveillance for outbreak detection, response and preparedness. Phylogenetic analysis of seven Marburg virus genomes from the 2025 outbreak in Ethiopia suggests human-to-human transmission after a spillover event.

title: Species-specific gene programs define divergent antiviral responses in Marburg virus reservoir bats and humans.
abstract: Bats tolerate viruses that cause severe disease in humans. Egyptian rousette bats, the natural reservoirs of Marburg virus (MARV), sustain asymptomatic infection, whereas humans develop severe and fatal disease. To define the basis of this divergence, we establish a comparative framework using primary and immortalized Egyptian rousette and human cells exposed to double-stranded RNA and interferon (IFN). Bat cells upregulate antiviral effectors while limiting inflammatory amplifiers, a pattern further supported by analysis of independent in vivo MARV infection datasets. In contrast, human cells activate antiviral programs and immune hyperactivation in response to MARV. Integrating transcriptomic and proteomic analyses, we identify species-specific immune programs encompassing differential IFN-stimulated gene regulation, apoptotic control, and cytokine signaling. Our findings establish an integrative framework for understanding species-specific antiviral responses associated with MARV reservoir biology, identify pathways linked to immunopathogenesis in humans, and provide a foundation for future studies of host responses to filovirus infection.

title: A Multi-Host Deterministic Model with Optimal Control Strategies for Marburg Virus Disease
abstract: Marburg virus disease (MVD) is a zoonotic viral haemorrhagic fever that presents continuing challenges for outbreak prevention and control. This study develops a deterministic compartmental model to examine transmission among humans, bats and monkeys, together with the contribution of environmental viral contamination. The human population is represented by susceptible, exposed, infectious, quarantined and recovered compartments, while susceptible and infected classes are considered for the animal hosts. The model incorporates direct and indirect transmission, quarantine, recovery, loss of immunity, and environmental viral shedding and decay. Non-negativity, boundedness, equilibria and reproduction-number thresholds are analysed. Latin hypercube sampling and sensitivity indices are used to examine parameter effects, while an optimal-control formulation evaluates quarantine and environmental interventions alongside behavioural responses. Under the assumed baseline parameters, model simulations indicate that environment-to-human exposure accounts for at least 99.3% of the human force of infection over the 50-day period. Environmental controls alone reduce the simulated infectious peak from 6.03 to 1.15 and the cumulative infectious burden by 85%. The combined intervention scenario produces the lowest reported objective value, although its infection trajectory is similar to that of environmental control alone. Increasing quarantine rates reduces simulated infectious peaks, whereas social distancing has limited influence in the environmentally dominated baseline scenario. These results underscore the importance of assessing multiple transmission routes when selecting interventions, while recognising that the findings depend on model structure and assumed parameter values.

title: Knowledge, perceptions, and associated factors of marburg virus disease in selected towns and districts of the South Ethiopia Region: an explanatory sequential mixed-methods study
abstract: The effectiveness of risk communication and community engagement (RCCE) depends on the population’s baseline knowledge, perceptions, and the sources of information. Therefore, this study aimed to assess community knowledge, perceptions, and associated factors of Marburg virus disease in the South Ethiopia Region. A community-based explanatory sequential mixed-methods study was employed among 614 adults in MVD-affected areas of the South Ethiopia Region from February 16, 2026, to March 10, 2026. Quantitative data were collected using interviewer-administered questionnaires with the Kobo Toolbox data collection software. For qualitative data, focus group discussions were conducted. To identify study participants, a systematic random sampling technique was used. To identify factors associated with knowledge and perception towards MVD, a binary logistic regression was fitted. Statistical significance was declared at a P -value < 0.05. For qualitative data, thematic content analysis was conducted. Among 611 adults who participated in the study, 74.8% (95% CI 71.2%, 78.1%) had good knowledge, and 62.7% (95% CI 58.8%, 66.4%) had positive perception, respectively. Educational status (AOR = 4.40; 95% CI 2.45, 7.89), source of information (AOR = 0.42; 95% CI 0.21, 0.87), and perception (AOR = 2.05; 95% CI 1.28, 3.26) were associated with knowledge. Participants aged 25–59 years (AOR = 0.40; 95% CI 0.21, 0.75), social media utilization (AOR = 5.13; 95% CI 3.12, 8.44), and MVD knowledge (AOR = 2.00; 95% CI 1.31, 3.0) were associated with perception. Health education delivered in multiple channels contributed to increased knowledge, whereas official recognition corrected early misconceptions and changed attitudes. Targeted interventions that focus on lower educational status and wealth, advanced age, and sources of information are essential. Strengthening risk communication and community engagement via trusted platforms is crucial. Strategies that utilize social media for information dissemination, empower housewives, and build positive perceptions are highly recommended.

title: A Synthetic Consensus Chiroptera IFN-β Induces IFN-I Signaling Across Diverse Bat Taxa
abstract: Bat-associated viruses consistently spill over from bats into humans and other animals. Many bat-associated viruses, including Marburg virus and Nipah virus, cause severe disease in humans but their presentation is subclinical in bats. Advancements in tools and resources to study bat innate antiviral immune responses, including the type I IFN (IFN-I) pathway, are needed to evaluate the mechanisms that underlie differential infection outcomes between reservoir bats and spillover hosts. Commercially available IFN-Is are not bat-specific, and conspecific IFN-Is are impractical to produce for the over 1,500 described bat species. Here, we design and validate a bat order-level consensus IFN (Chiroptera IFN-β) that is functional in bat cells from six diverse bat families, including representatives from both suborders. Using Jamaican fruit bat cells, we demonstrate that Chiroptera IFN-β induces an IFN-stimulated gene repertoire comparable to conspecific IFN-β. This valuable resource can accelerate the capacity of the field to study bat innate antiviral responses and illuminate differences between bats and humans.

title: Ebola virus transmission among healthcare workers: genomic epidemiological analysis of the 2014 Kenema Government Hospital outbreak
abstract: Abstract Background During the 2014 Ebola outbreak in Sierra Leone, widespread infections among healthcare workers at Kenema Government Hospital severely disrupted clinical operations. Whether these infections primarily arose from repeated patient exposures or from transmission among colleagues remained unclear, particularly as patient admissions exceeded the hospital’s capacity for safe isolation and care. Methods We revisited the outbreak using expanded viral surveillance and classical genomic analysis, Bayesian transmission inference with juniper , and firsthand epidemiologic accounts from hospital staff. We analyzed 279 Ebola virus genomes from Kenema District, including 35 from infected healthcare workers, and 514 genomes in the broader transmission reconstruction, explicitly accounting for unsampled cases. Results The 35 healthcare worker genomes comprised 28 haplotypes, including five shared by multiple cases. In the reconstructed transmission network, 22 candidate healthcare worker-to-healthcare worker links exceeded a posterior probability threshold of 5%, representing 6.1-fold enrichment over expectation. Healthcare workers accounted for 33.2% of expected onward transmissions at their peak in the two-week window beginning June 23, 2014. Firsthand anecdotal accounts situated inferred relationships within specific wards, clinical procedures, and working relationships of KGH, including care of infected colleagues and infections among laboratory, pharmacy, and other personnel beyond routine bedside care. Conclusions Ebola transmission involved interconnected groups of healthcare workers across multiple hospital departments during a period of severe resource constraints and expanding patient demand. These findings underscore the importance of protecting and surveilling healthcare workers as an interconnected workforce during emerging outbreaks.

title: Dialysis Toolkit for Ebola Virus Disease-Associated Acute Kidney Injury
abstract: Ebola virus disease (EVD), a high-fatality haemorrhagic fever endemic to Central and West Africa. EVD frequently presents with multiorgan dysfunction, including acute kidney injury (AKI). The management of AKI in EVD presents unique challenges owing to the infection’s highly contagious nature, the need for critical care in low-resource environments, and the logistics of providing kidney replacement therapy (KRT) in high-biohazard settings. This manuscript outlines a “dialysis toolkit” to guide clinicians managing AKI in EVD. This toolkit covers infection control protocols, preferred KRT modalities, anticoagulation strategies, effluent disposal, and machine handling. Based on existing literature and biosafety guidance, this toolkit is intended for nephrologists, intensivists, intensive care unit nurses, dialysis nurses, infection-prevention teams, and biomedical staff. With this article, we aim to balance optimal nephrological care with maximal protection for healthcare workers across both resource-rich and austere outbreak settings. Keywords: Acute kidney injury, Ebola virus disease, Dialysis, Hemodialysis, Kidney replacement therapy, Peritoneal dialysis.

title: A bivalent Lassa virus mRNA vaccine protects guinea pigs from lethal infection with Lassa virus
abstract: Abstract: Lassa virus (LASV), the causative agent of the life-threatening febrile disease, Lassa fever, remains a major public health concern in West Africa, where hundreds of thousands of infections occur annually. However, no licensed vaccine is currently available, highlighting the urgent need for effective preventive measures. We previously demonstrated that an mRNA-lipid nanoparticle (LNP) vaccine expressing LASV glycoprotein precursor (GPC; LASgpc-mRNA-LNP) conferred protection against lethal infection with a recombinant lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus expressing LASV GPC in mice. In this study, we extended our previous work with the aim of evaluating the efficacy of an mRNA-LNP vaccine expressing LASV nucleoprotein (NP; LASnp-mRNA-LNP) and a bivalent vaccine combining LASgpc-mRNA-LNP and LASnp-mRNA-LNP. Using a lethal CBA/N mouse model of infection with ML29, an LASV live-attenuated vaccine candidate encoding LASV GPC and NP, we found that LASgpc-mRNA-LNP and LASnp-mRNA-LNP each conferred protection in the absence of detectable neutralizing antibody responses. We identified LASV GPC- and NP-derived CD4+ and CD8+ T-cell epitope peptides in CBA/N mice and demonstrated that vaccination induced robust antigen-specific T-cell responses. Importantly, the bivalent vaccine provided complete protection against lethal challenge with doses at which monovalent vaccines failed to protect all mice, suggesting a potential dose-sparing benefit of the bivalent formulation. Furthermore, the bivalent vaccine fully protected guinea pigs against lethal challenge with authentic LASV. Together, these findings establish LASV NP, in addition to GPC, as a protective antigen in the mRNA vaccine platform and provide a rationale for developing bivalent mRNA-LNP vaccines to improve protection against Lassa fever. One Sentence Summary A bivalent mRNA-LNP vaccine expressing Lassa virus GPC and NP confers robust protection against lethal Lassa virus infection

title: Quantifying the extinction probability of Marburg virus disease outbreaks: A continuous-time Markov chain model integrating a multi-type branching process
abstract: Understanding the extinction dynamics of Marburg virus disease is crucial, particularly during the early stages of an outbreak when stochastic effects strongly influence disease outcomes. Although deterministic models have provided valuable insights into virus transmission dynamics, they cannot adequately capture random transmission events or quantify extinction probabilities, particularly when outbreaks begin with few infected cases. This study develops a continuous-time Markov chain stochastic model derived from a deterministic multi-host transmission model. The model incorporates a multi-type branching process, in which distinct infectious types are tracked according to their contributions to secondary infections, enabling estimation of disease extinction probabilities during the early outbreak phase. The extinction analysis shows that outbreaks initiated by exposed humans have a higher probability of extinction (21.6%) compared with those initiated by infectious humans (13.7%), whereas outbreaks initiated by infected bats have an extinction probability of only 0.36%, highlighting their role as important reservoirs sustaining virus transmission. Furthermore, the results demonstrate that reducing human-to-human transmission, decreasing viral shedding, and increasing environmental viral decay significantly enhance the likelihood of disease extinction. The proposed framework provides a quantitative tool for assessing Marburg virus disease outbreak risk and valuable insights for designing early interventions for human transmission, environmental contamination, and cross-species interactions.

title_zh: 量化马尔堡病毒病 暴发的灭绝概率:一种整合多类型分支过程的连续时间马尔可夫链模型
source_body_en: Understanding the extinction dynamics of Marburg virus disease is crucial, particularly during the early stages of an outbreak when stochastic effects strongly influence disease outcomes. Although deterministic models have provided valuable insights into virus transmission dynamics, they cannot adequately capture random transmission events or quantify extinction probabilities, particularly when outbreaks begin with few infected cases. This study develops a continuous-time Markov chain stochastic model derived from a deterministic multi-host transmission model. The model incorporates a multi-type branching process, in which distinct infectious types are tracked according to their contributions to secondary infections, enabling estimation of disease extinction probabilities during the early outbreak phase. The extinction analysis shows that outbreaks initiated by exposed humans have a higher probability of extinction (21.6%) compared with those initiated by infectious humans (13.7%), whereas outbreaks initiated by infected bats have an extinction probability of only 0.36%, highlighting their role as important reservoirs sustaining virus transmission. Furthermore, the results demonstrate that reducing human-to-human transmission, decreasing viral shedding, and increasing environmental viral decay significantly enhance the likelihood of disease extinction. The proposed framework provides a quantitative tool for assessing Marburg virus disease outbreak risk and valuable insights for designing early interventions for human transmission, environmental contamination, and cross-species interactions.
abstract_zh: 理解马尔堡病毒病的灭绝动力学至关重要,尤其是在暴发初期阶段,随机效应对疾病结果有显著影响。尽管确定性模型为病毒传播动力学提供了有价值的见解,但它们无法充分捕捉随机传播事件或量化灭绝概率,特别是在暴发初始病例较少时。本研究基于一个确定性多宿主 传播模型,开发了一个连续时间马尔可夫链随机模型。该模型采用多类型分支过程,根据不同感染类型对二次感染的贡献进行追踪,从而能够在暴发初期阶段估计疾病灭绝概率。灭绝分析表明,由暴露人类引发的暴发灭绝概率为21.6%,高于由传染性人类引发的暴发(13.7%),而由感染蝙蝠引发的暴发灭绝概率仅为0.36%,突显了蝙蝠作为重要储存宿主维持病毒传播的作用。此外,研究结果表明,减少人传人传播、降低病毒排毒量以及增加环境病毒衰减显著提高了疾病灭绝的可能性。所提出的框架为评估马尔堡病毒病 暴发风险提供了定量工具,并为设计针对人类传播、环境污染和跨物种互动的早期干预措施提供了有价值的见解。

title: Constructing event graph and mining critical paths of Ebola virus disease: a public health emergency analysis based on WHO disease outbreak news
abstract:
Background

Most Ebola virus disease research focuses on clinical diagnosis or static knowledge networks, limiting dynamic spatiotemporal analysis of epidemic evolution. We examined whether an event graph derived from World Health Organization (WHO) Disease Outbreak News (DONs) could reconstruct outbreak evolution across reports and identify response-timing patterns, including delayed interventions, unactioned risk assessments, and cross-border escalation.

Methods

We retrospectively analysed 346 Ebola-related DON reports published through August 2025. We used a large language model-assisted framework to extract events and their relationships. We built an event graph in Neo4j and applied a bounded depth-first search procedure that removed cycles, generated candidate paths, and selected critical paths across six dimensions: case burden, spatial spread, international risk signals, intervention measures, path length, and graph structural importance.

Results

The graph comprised 2233 event nodes and 10,479 relations across 155 event groups; 47 representative critical paths were selected. Laboratory confirmation often marked the shift from uncertain signals to an organised response. Healthcare-facility exposure and community deaths served as sentinel events for infection-control review and transmission-chain investigation. Preparedness, surveillance, and contact tracing generally followed spatial spread and international-risk signals rather than general border restrictions. Repeated burden updates without documented interventions indicated potential response or reporting gaps. Although established control measures aligned with WHO advice, the report defined explicit triggers, deadlines, inter-agency handoffs, and completion indicators less clearly.

Conclusions

The event graph reconstructed longitudinal outbreak and response trajectories that are difficult to capture through descriptive summaries or entity-centred knowledge graphs. Effective Ebola response depends not only on available control measures but also on activating them at appropriate transition points. This framework complements, rather than replaces, WHO guidance, real-time surveillance, and formal epidemiological causal inference.

METHODSData sourcesWe used an observational study design, including a secondary (retrospective) data analysis. We sourced the data from the WHO Emergency Events Webpage's DONs. The WHO system compiles and continuously updates this data source [16,17], which includes records of various public health emergencies globally, including infectious disease outbreaks, conflicts, and natural disasters. It serves as an authoritative and reliable resource for public health analysis. Each report includes essential information, such as the nature of the emergency, the affected country or region, the incident report date, the degree of health hazard, and the response measures implemented by the WHO. The transparency and accessibility of the data provide a robust foundation for this study. We used web crawler technology for data collection. Initially, we collected all reports of public health events related to virus outbreaks on the WHO emergency event page, then focused on the Ebola virus outbreak for topic screening. Ultimately, we obtained 346 effective report texts as the foundational data sources for subsequent information extraction.We included all reports of human EVD outbreaks published on the WHO emergency website through August 2025. We excluded reports of infections not caused by Ebola virus, animal infection events without documented human transmission, and duplicate reports with identical or substantially overlapping content.The reports share a similar structure, primarily comprising the following sections: situation description, detailed description, public health response, WHO risk assessment, epidemiology, and further information. The initial report's content module is relatively straightforward, whereas the subsequent reports are more comprehensive. During data preprocessing, we uniformly removed the ‘supplementary information’ section from all reports, as it contained only links to other information, had no analytical value, and did not substantively affect subsequent research. Concurrently, we removed redundant blank lines from the reports, retaining only core analytical content to ensure data consistency and validity.Information extractionThe concept of event and relationshipIn the theoretical framework of event graph research, an event is defined as an objective state change or factual occurrence triggered by one or more agents through a specific action or process within a defined spatiotemporal scope [18,19]. Its core features are semantic integrity and structured expression, the basic semantic units that support logical relationship modelling between events. From a formal perspective, an event can be represented as a multi-tuple form: E = (e_id, T, S, A, P, Attr), where e_id is the unique identifier of the event, T is the time attribute (including the start time t_start and the end time t_end), S is the spatial attribute (including the geographical scope and hierarchy), A is the set of participants (A = {a_1, a_2, ..., a_n}; each participant is associated with a specific semantic role), P is the description of the core action or state change, Attr is the set of event attributes (including key features such as event type, polarity, and tense). This definition not only continues the classical definition of the core elements of events in the field of event semantic modelling [20], but also realises the structured encapsulation of semantic information through the multi-group form, which can accurately describe the dynamic characteristics and composition logic of events in the fields of public health and disaster emergency. It provides a unified semantic basis for extracting and modelling causal, temporal, and conditional relationships between events in the event graph and ensures systematic representation of event-association logic.Combining the characteristics of unstructured text event extraction and the requirements of event graph construction, the public health event defined in this research is: in a specific domain context, the semantic unit activated by the trigger word can reflect the core dynamic facts, and the formal representation still uses the multivariate group E = (e_id, T, S, A, P, Attr), but it is necessary to clarify the difference between this definition and the traditional standard event definition. Because event information is derived directly from unstructured text, it is affected by ambiguous descriptions and missing information. The extracted event does not need to contain all tuple elements. The core only needs to retain the core action/process P corresponding to the trigger word and the key semantic elements to ensure that the event has distinguishability and relationship modelling capabilities. This definition not only preserves events' essential characteristics as dynamic semantic units, but also adapts to the practical needs of unstructured text information extraction, providing a flexible, rigorous basis for constructing event correlations in the event graph.Based on the definition of the above events, we also explain the relationship between events. The relationship between events is roughly divided into three categories:1. Causality: refers to the cause-effect association between event E1 and E2 [21,22], wherein E1 directly affects the probability of E2 occurring by changing the preconditions of the event, rather than the two events merely co-occurring in time. The tangible manifestation of this relationship is an action or information-flow chain that connects E1 and E2, such that changes to E1 affect the likelihood of E2 occurring. In text and natural language processing, causality is expressed through a cause-effect link, requiring that E1 precede and influence E2.2. Sequential: events follow a temporal sequence [23]. E1 occurs before E2; however, this does not imply that E1 causally influences the emergence of E2. Rather, it represents a purely temporal association distinct from causality. This relationship is classified into two forms: strict succession (wherein one event initiates immediately upon the termination of another) and loose succession. Its fundamental characteristic is temporal sequentiality, in which one event occurs after another.3. Parallel: indicates that there is neither a causal relationship nor a dependent sequential step between events that typically occur simultaneously or exist as independent branches of the same process [24]. Although such events may share overarching contexts or common causes, they do not influence one another. In the analysis, these events can be associated with a ‘relational event history’ or parallel sequences, but they do not demonstrate a clear causal direction.Event extractionTechnological evolution in the field of natural language processing has shown that the language representation ability constructed by large language models (LLMs) through self-supervised learning has achieved state-of-the-art performance in natural language understanding and natural language generation tasks [25], which can effectively solve the problem of accurately extracting key information in unstructured epidemic texts. This study employs DeepSeek-R1 – a large language model with enhanced reasoning capabilities via the chain-of-thought approach – as the core tool for event and relation extraction thought [26,27] (Appendix S1 in the Online Supplementary Document). The chain-of-thought mechanism further improves the model's ability to infer logical relationships in complex events by simulating humans' gradual reasoning process and provides reliable support for event classification and relationship determination [28]. The event extraction workflow comprised text cleaning, event extraction, temporal ordering, entity standardisation, and format unification (Figure 1, Panel A).Figure 1Technical frameworks for event and event-relation extraction. Panel A. Event extraction framework. Panel B. Event-relation extraction framework. CoT – chain-of-thought, LLM – large language model.The framework initially establishes the model as an 'epidemic text normalisation expert,' constraining the output to structured results without requiring additional analysis or interpretation and adhering strictly to the predefined example format. The first step involves text cleaning, which removes non-essential web navigation content and keeps only the first occurrence of duplicate data. The second step extracts events from the text based on the event's defined elements. The third step organises the event sequence using temporal markers such as dates and ‘epidemic X week’ as anchor points, and restructures the text into the ‘time: event content’ format to prevent word-order confusion. The next step is entity alignment, which standardises the three core entity names, institutions, virus terms, and countries/regions, using predefined mapping rules. The next step unifies the format and converts the time to the ‘YYYY-MM-DD’ standard format. Finally, the process concludes with event element extraction, identifying and extracting all recognisable components defined by the multi-tuple representation E = (e_id, T, S, A, P, Attr) to the fullest extent possible. The extracted elements encompass temporal attributes (T), spatial attributes (S), participant sets (A), core action descriptions (P), and supplementary attributes (Attr) including event type, polarity, and tense. Given the ambiguous and incomplete nature of unstructured epidemic text, we do not artificially supplement tuple elements absent from the original content; we retain only verifiable semantic elements to ensure event distinguishability and enable subsequent event relation modelling. To provide in-context guidance for event extraction, we manually annotated five WHO DONs reports and incorporated them into the prompt as few-shot examples. These examples illustrated the expected event boundaries, temporal normalisation, entity standardisation, and structured output format. We did not update any model parameters; the annotated examples served solely as prompt-based guidance to improve the consistency of model outputs (Appendix S2 in the Online Supplementary Document).Event relation extractionConsidering the event set results, we also need to ascertain the interrelationships among these events. Event-relation extraction combines event-type recognition, candidate-relation matching, report-level association verification, and final relation determination (Figure 1, Panel B).First, to enable a more comprehensive examination of the outbreak's critical path, we categorised epidemic events into six distinct types. These categories are delineated as:− Early epidemic events: occurring in the early stage of an epidemic, characterised by the emergence of signs of human-to-human Ebola virus transmission, the reporting of sporadic suspected cases in local areas, and no identified clear transmission chain or large-scale community transmission.− Epidemic outbreak events: rapid expansion of the scope of virus transmission, exponential growth of the number of infected people beyond the local prevention and control carrying capacity, and the formation of a cross-regional transmission trend of related events.− Case report events: relevant events of the discovery, registration, statistics, and publicity of suspected cases, confirmed cases, and deaths of Ebola by medical and health institutions, disease control departments, or relevant organisations.− Epidemic response events: related to prevention and control measures, such as entry and exit control, epidemic area blockade, personnel isolation, and public health publicity implemented by governments and international organisations in response to the Ebola epidemic.− Medical intervention events: medical-related events such as clinical treatment, vaccination, drug development and application, and medical resource allocation for Ebola-infected patients.− Epidemic termination events: denote the formal declaration of the conclusion of the epidemic.To improve the LLM's ability to discern event relationships and support consistent relation extraction, we constructed an empirical event type–candidate relation matrix based on repeated observations of event sequences in WHO DON reports and preliminary extraction results. This matrix was not intended to represent a formal ontology or expert consensus. Instead, it served as a heuristic guide to narrow the plausible candidate relations between ordered event-type pairs. The matrix alone did not determine the final relation label; local textual evidence, temporal order, and the contextual meaning of the two events did. This matrix uses the six event-type combinations above and posits Sequential, Causality, and Parallel relationships between them (Table 1). The matrix guides the LLM to combine event-type and contextual semantics when determining event relationships, improving the rationality of relation extraction.Table 1Event type–candidate relation matrixCombinations of event typesSequential relationshipCausality relationshipParallel relationshipEarly epidemic events→ epidemic outbreak eventsInitial→outbreak (time successively)Initially lead to an outbreak (causality) Epidemic outbreak events → case report eventsOutbreak → report (time successively)Outbreak pushes report (causality) Epidemic outbreak events → Epidemic response eventsOutbreak → response (time successively)Outbreak triggers response (causality)Parallel occurrence (parallel)Epidemic outbreak events → medical intervention eventsOutbreak → intervention (time successively)Outbreak pushes intervention (causality) Case report events→ epidemic response eventsReport → Response (time successively)Data drives response (causality)Parallel occurrence (parallel)Case report events → epidemic termination eventsReport → End (time successively)Ended with data proof (causality) Epidemic response events → medical intervention eventsThere is compliance (response → intervention) in some scenes Parallel occurrence (parallel)Epidemic response events → epidemic termination eventsResponse → end (time successively)Response pushed to end (causality) Medical intervention events → epidemic termination eventsIntervention → end (time successively)Intervention drives the end (cause and effect)Subsequently, the LLM (DeepSeek-R1) uses a four-step reasoning framework for relation extraction. It must accurately identify four types of associations between events: ‘causality, sequential, parallel, and unrelated’. The initial step involves event type recognition, which is achieved through ‘core action + occurrence stage’ feature matching to clarify the event type. The second step entails correlation verification. If the two events originate from the same report, they are deemed highly correlated, and the predefined relationship is preferentially referenced and assessed. Otherwise, in the absence of a clear correlation clue, the events are initially considered to have 'low correlation'. The third step involves predefined relationship matching, where inference rules are constructed based on event-type combination logic, and decisions are derived by querying the corresponding event type–candidate relation matrix. The fourth step involves relationship determination. By synthesising the outcomes of the preceding three steps, the model identifies the final relationship type and outputs only the relationship category. full_text_sections.results: RESULTSDescriptive statistical resultsWe performed a descriptive statistical analysis on the extracted data. This research manually summarised the 346 Ebola-related DONs reports by country. Reports were unevenly distributed, with the Democratic Republic of the Congo contributing the most (Figure 2).Figure 2Number of Ebola-related DON reports by country. DON – Disease Outbreak News.In this study, among the 346 EVD reports, the outbreak's spatial distribution showed significant regional clustering and high-frequency activity. The Democratic Republic of the Congo was the most frequently represented country in the corpus, accounting for 141 of the 346 reports (40.8%). These findings align closely with the long-term monitoring conclusions of the WHO and the United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Uganda ranked second with 56 outbreak-related reports, most of which involved Sudan ebolavirus outbreaks. Historical regional epidemics underscore East Africa's risk profile as a hotspot for cross-species virus transmission. Guinea and Gabon ranked third and fourth, with 40 and 34 reports, respectively.Results of information extractionThe LLM-assisted extraction procedure generated structured event records containing event descriptions, event dates, and corresponding source reports (Table S1 in the Online Supplementary Document). Based on these records, representative event-pair outputs illustrate how the model assigned relation labels according to the temporal and contextual associations between events (Table S2 in the Online Supplementary Document).To evaluate the reliability of the model-based information extraction, this study manually validated a random sample of 20 WHO DON reports and 100 event pairs. For event extraction, the two reviewers manually identified 132 event units from the selected reports. The LLM extracted 118 event units from the same reports, of which 94 were judged to be consistent with the manually identified events. The event extraction precision was 79.66%, recall was 71.21%, and F1 was 75.20%. For event relation extraction, we randomly selected 100 event pairs and manually reviewed them. Of these, 78 relation labels assigned by the model matched manual judgment, yielding an overall relation classification accuracy of 78.00% (Table 2). The model performed relatively well in identifying Sequential relations, while most errors occurred in distinguishing Causality from Sequential relations. This confusion was particularly common when the report described a response action following an outbreak update, but did not explicitly state a causality connection.Table 2Manual validation results of model-based information extractionPerformance, % Validation task Manual sample size Model output Correct/matched results Precision Recall F1 Accuracy Event extraction132 manually identified events from 20 reports118 extracted events94 matched events79.6671.2175.20 Relation extraction100 event pairs100 model-assigned relations78 correct relation labels78.00F1 – harmonic mean of precision and recallOverall, the validation results indicate that the LLM-assisted extraction method provided a usable but imperfect structured basis for constructing the Ebola event graph. The model captured most major public health events, but omissions and boundary inconsistencies remained in complex report paragraphs. Therefore, we needed to consolidate outbreak-level events, remove duplicates, correct relations, and remove cycles before critical path mining.Results of graph constructionA partial view of the constructed event graph illustrates the temporal organisation of event nodes and the causal, sequential, and parallel relations among them (Figure 3). Before critical path mining, the initial relation data set contained 8919 records. We added 1749 new relations generated during event cluster consolidation, bringing the total to 10,668 relational records. Two records with blank relation labels were excluded, leaving 10,666 typed relations. After temporal correction and cycle removal, the final graph contained 10,479 relations: 4075 Causality, 3707 Sequential, and 2697 Parallel. full_text_sections.discussion: DISCUSSIONPath resultsAnalysis of the 47 representative critical paths reveals several recurrent response patterns that event frequency or path length alone cannot explain. First, laboratory confirmation served as a transition from uncertain outbreak signals to an organised response: laboratory-confirmation milestones appeared in 27 paths, and 20 of these were followed by a subsequent non-laboratory intervention, indicating that the critical interval extended from specimen collection and testing to notification, isolation, contact tracing, and field action. Second, healthcare facilities served as both response sites and potential transmission amplifiers. Healthcare-facility-related events appeared in 27 paths, and 18 were followed by later intervention milestones, suggesting that healthcare-worker infection, delayed recognition, or movement between facilities should be treated as sentinel evidence of possible triage or infection-prevention failure. Third, death was not simply the terminal outcome of a path. full_text_sections.conclusion: CONCLUSIONSWe proposed an event-graph-based framework to address the limited ability of conventional descriptive summaries and entity-centred knowledge graphs to reconstruct how Ebola outbreaks evolve across successive reports. By linking fragmented outbreak signals, transmission-related events, risk assessments, and response actions into ordered event chains, the framework provides a more structured representation of how reported outbreaks and public-health responses evolve over time, rather than relying on static aggregation of information. The critical-path evaluation further distinguishes epidemiologically meaningful event chains by disease burden, spatial spread, international risk, intervention measures, path length, and structural importance.The findings indicate that an effective Ebola response depends not only on the availability of established control measures, but also on activating these measures at appropriate transition points. Laboratory confirmation, healthcare-worker infection, community deaths, spatial spread, and elevated risk assessments emerged as important signals requiring coordinated follow-up. Comparison with WHO advice showed that existing recommendations generally cover the principal Ebola-control measures, but provide less consistent detail on when specific signals should trigger action, how rapidly responses should begin, how responsibilities should be transferred across teams or administrative boundaries, and how implementation should be verified. Accordingly, this study recommends linking key outbreak signals to predefined, time-bound, auditable response procedures; strengthening coordination among surveillance, laboratory, clinical, burial, contact-tracing, and cross-border teams; and establishing alerts for potential response or documentation gaps.Overall, the event-graph framework complements rather than replaces WHO guidance, real-time surveillance, or formal epidemiological causal inference. Its main contribution is transforming fragmented outbreak reports into interpretable response trajectories and identifying operational points at which established control measures should be initiated, coordinated, and monitored. Future research should incorporate broader surveillance and graphical sources, strengthen expert validation, and evaluate the framework's robustness and generalisability across different outbreaks and reporting systems.
full_text_sections.other: Data sourcesWe used an observational study design, including a secondary (retrospective) data analysis. We sourced the data from the WHO Emergency Events Webpage's DONs. The WHO system compiles and continuously updates this data source [16,17], which includes records of various public health emergencies globally, including infectious disease outbreaks, conflicts, and natural disasters. It serves as an authoritative and reliable resource for public health analysis. Each report includes essential information, such as the nature of the emergency, the affected country or region, the incident report date, the degree of health hazard, and the response measures implemented by the WHO. The transparency and accessibility of the data provide a robust foundation for this study. We used web crawler technology for data collection. Initially, we collected all reports of public health events related to virus outbreaks on the WHO emergency event page, then focused on the Ebola virus outbreak for topic screening. Ultimately, we obtained 346 effective report texts as the foundational data sources for subsequent information extraction.We included all reports of human EVD outbreaks published on the WHO emergency website through August 2025. We excluded reports of infections not caused by Ebola virus, animal infection events without documented human transmission, and duplicate reports with identical or substantially overlapping content.The reports share a similar structure, primarily comprising the following sections: situation description, detailed description, public health response, WHO risk assessment, epidemiology, and further information. The initial report's content module is relatively straightforward, whereas the subsequent reports are more comprehensive. During data preprocessing, we uniformly removed the ‘supplementary information’ section from all reports, as it contained only links to other information, had no analytical value, and did not substantively affect subsequent research. Concurrently, we removed redundant blank lines from the reports, retaining only core analytical content to ensure data consistency and validity. Information extractionThe concept of event and relationshipIn the theoretical framework of event graph research, an event is defined as an objective state change or factual occurrence triggered by one or more agents through a specific action or process within a defined spatiotemporal scope [18,19]. Its core features are semantic integrity and structured expression, the basic semantic units that support logical relationship modelling between events. From a formal perspective, an event can be represented as a multi-tuple form: E = (e_id, T, S, A, P, Attr), where e_id is the unique identifier of the event, T is the time attribute (including the start time t_start and the end time t_end), S is the spatial attribute (including the geographical scope and hierarchy), A is the set of participants (A = {a_1, a_2, ..., a_n}; each participant is associated with a specific semantic role), P is the description of the core action or state change, Attr is the set of event attributes (including key features such as event type, polarity, and tense). This definition not only continues the classical definition of the core elements of events in the field of event semantic modelling [20], but also realises the structured encapsulation of semantic information through the multi-group form, which can accurately describe the dynamic characteristics and composition logic of events in the fields of public health and disaster emergency. It provides a unified semantic basis for extracting and modelling causal, temporal, and conditional relationships between events in the event graph and ensures systematic representation of event-association logic.Combining the characteristics of unstructured text event extraction and the requirements of event graph construction, the public health event defined in this research is: in a specific domain context, the semantic unit activated by the trigger word can reflect the core dynamic facts, and the formal representation still uses the multivariate group E = (e_id, T, S, A, P, Attr), but it is necessary to clarify the difference between this definition and the traditional standard event definition. Because event information is derived directly from unstructured text, it is affected by ambiguous descriptions and missing information. The extracted event does not need to contain all tuple elements. The core only needs to retain the core action/process P corresponding to the trigger word and the key semantic elements to ensure that the event has distinguishability and relationship modelling capabilities. This definition not only preserves events' essential characteristics as dynamic semantic units, but also adapts to the practical needs of unstructured text information extraction, providing a flexible, rigorous basis for constructing event correlations in the event graph.Based on the definition of the above events, we also explain the relationship between events. The relationship between events is roughly divided into three categories:1. Causality: refers to the cause-effect association between event E1 and E2 [21,22], wherein E1 directly affects the probability of E2 occurring by changing the preconditions of the event, rather than the two events merely co-occurring in time. The tangible manifestation of this relationship is an action or information-flow chain that connects E1 and E2, such that changes to E1 affect the likelihood of E2 occurring. In text and natural language processing, causality is expressed through a cause-effect link, requiring that E1 precede and influence E2.2. Sequential: events follow a temporal sequence [23]. E1 occurs before E2; however, this does not imply that E1 causally influences the emergence of E2. Rather, it represents a purely temporal association distinct from causality. This relationship is classified into two forms: strict succession (wherein one event initiates immediately upon the termination of another) and loose succession. Its fundamental characteristic is temporal sequentiality, in which one event occurs after another.3. Parallel: indicates that there is neither a causal relationship nor a dependent sequential step between events that typically occur simultaneously or exist as independent branches of the same process [24]. Although such events may share overarching contexts or common causes, they do not influence one another. full_text: AbstractMulti-pathogen and combination vaccines are vaccines that deliver antigens from two or more pathogens in a single shot to protect against multiple diseases. This can include several individual vaccines formulated together to be delivered as a single shot as well as multivalent vaccines, where a single vaccine expresses or contains multiple antigens. Multi-pathogen vaccines present an obvious solution for rapidly protecting a population against multiple biological threat agents simultaneously. They also have additional cost and logistical advantages over delivering separate vaccines. However, data from childhood combination vaccines have shown that they do not always perform as the sum of their parts, so ensuring that newly developed multi-pathogen vaccines protect as well as their individual vaccine counterparts can be challenging. Here, we focus on three core mechanisms of vaccine interference; epitope competition, resource competition and immune polarization, and discuss how multi-pathogen vaccines across different platforms (viral vectors, bacterial vectors, protein/subunit and nucleic acid) are impacted by each mechanism. We review multi-pathogen vaccines in development for pathogens and toxins that pose a biological threat, and propose an evaluation metric for assessing potential adverse combinations of vaccines. This review is intended to provide information relevant for platform-selection for developing biodefense vaccines for stockpiling and rapid deployment.Keywords: biodefense, biothreat, combination vaccines, multi-pathogen, multivalent, vaccine interference, vaccines 8.MethodsPubMed, a scholarly repository of journal articles about health and medicine, was searched with the terms in Figure 2 through July 2025. The list of biodefense-relevant pathogens (and wider viral families) was taken from the CDC bioterrorism agent list (9). The specific search terms are shown in Figure 2 and were searched in combination, where each of the first terms “Vaccine term” were combined with each of the second terms “Pathogen terms”. This process yielded duplicates (i.e. a Lassa, Marburg and Ebola multi-pathogen vaccine appears three times), which are not removed from the search totals. The search results were manually filtered. Records were removed if they; did not pertain to pathogen vaccines; did not pertain to the pathogens identified by the CDC bioterrorism agent list; or only included vaccination against a single species/virus. Multiple reviewers were involved in the screening process in determining the final set of articles. Additional articles providing relevant mechanisms and broader immunology were searched using PubMed but without systematic screening.Figure 2Schematic of search methodology. * indicates duplicates.Flowchart illustrating a PubMed literature search strategy for multipathogen vaccines, listing vaccine and pathogen terms used for querying. Records identified: 1,208; screened: 1,208; assessed for eligibility: 147; included: 42. Exclusion reasons are detailed. Supplementary materialThe Supplementary Material for this article can be found online at: https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fimmu.2026.1945700/full#supplementary-material Supplementary Materials 9.DiscussionIt is difficult to predict how vaccines will interact in combination or within multivalent formulations, though some interference mechanisms are platform-specific. Table 1 groups vaccines by platform to indicate which mechanisms should be considered when assessing co-administered or multi-pathogen vaccines.Streamlining the development of multi-pathogen vaccines requires attention to three key areas: (1) experimental designs that allow for direct comparison with previous effective or protective single-pathogen vaccines; (2) mechanistic understanding of platform-related challenges; and (3) characterization of immune polarization. Each of these considerations is expanded upon below:Experimental design for comparisons. A practical development sequence should begin with in vitro confirmation that each antigen is expressed at the expected level when delivered alone and in combination, followed by optimization of antigen dose and ratio to minimize competition while maintaining protective responses to each pathogen. Candidate formulations should then be evaluated using standardized immune-response assays and predefined, pathogen-appropriate correlates of protection, where available. This staged approach prioritizes relatively rapid antigen-expression and compatibility testing before resource-intensive animal studies, although dose adjustments or platform modifications may increase formulation complexity and may not fully predict immune interactions in vivo. Inclusion of monovalent or single-antigen counterparts as controls for multivalent vaccines is essential to enable direct comparison with existing datasets. If experimental constraints limit the number of test groups, standardized assay formats should be used (e.g., normalizing antibody titers to a known monoclonal). These considerations align with broader calls for standardized immunogenicity metrics, harmonized experimental protocols, and transparent reporting to improve comparability across vaccine studies (117). The experimental design should replicate conditions used in single-vaccine experiments including animal age, vaccine dose and volume, challenge details, and timepoints.Platform-specific challenges. Different vaccine platforms and vectors have unique challenges when delivered as combinations. For example, multi-pathogen DNA vaccines may encounter plasmid competition. Similarly, protein expression interference or co-infection limitations in nucleic acid and viral vectored vaccines can be empirically determined with in vitro assays that reduce the need for in vivo testing of potentially incompatible vaccines.Immune polarization effects. Combining vaccines or antigens can alter cellular immune polarization leading to shifts in antibody isotypes and downstream cellular responses. One proposed mechanism for impaired Hib responses in childhood combination vaccines (Hib and DTaP) involves the difference in adjuvant formulations: Hib vaccination does not contain an adjuvant, and the DTaP formulation contains aluminum salt (110). Although this mechanism is debated (111), vaccine assessment should include polarization metrics relevant to the animal model, such as IgG1/IgG2a ratios in BALB/c mice.As with single pathogen vaccines, results in one animal model are not guaranteed to translate to another, and immuno-bridging from animal models to human protection remains a significant challenge. For example, the bivalent Ad-vector ChAdOx1-biEBOV protected mice from both EBOV and SUDV challenge but failed to protect NHPs from SUDV challenge despite inducing robust humoral immunity. These findings underscore the importance of evaluating vaccine candidates in multiple models. The predictive value of an animal model depends on the pathogen, the extent to which the challenge reproduces human infection, and whether relevant correlates of protection are known. Species-specific differences in antigen processing, immune polarization, and effector responses, together with differences in challenge strain, dose, route, and study endpoint, can complicate interpretation. Multi-pathogen vaccine studies should therefore assess protection against each component individually and interpret immune responses within the limitations of the selected model.Multi-pathogen vaccines represent a promising strategy for biodefense research. When appropriately formulated, multi-pathogen vaccines could mitigate the threat posed by multiple biodefense pathogens while serving as a deterrent against the deliberate use of biological agents. In addition, multi-pathogen vaccines could reduce costs, streamline logistics, and shorten timelines for deployment. Careful consideration of vaccine interference will be critical to ensure accurate assessment of vaccine quality and to accelerate the development of effective biodefense vaccines. A unified evaluation framework for multi-pathogen biodefense vaccines should therefore progress from in vitro antigen-expression and compatibility testing, to dose and antigen-ratio optimization, and standardized comparison with monovalent controls. Changing the vaccine platform may resolve expression- or vector-specific interference but requires more extensive redevelopment and validation. In an ideal scenario, comparisons across species should use matched antigen amino acid sequences, formulations, doses scaled using a clearly defined rationale, sampling timepoints, challenge conditions, and immune-response assays. Safety assessment should also examine whether subprotective or imbalanced responses increase risks such as antibody-dependent enhancement, enhanced disease, or accelerated mortality following challenge. Applying this framework to vaccines targeting Category A–C biothreat agents would support transparent selection of candidates for stockpiling based on breadth of protection, durability, safety, manufacturability, and readiness for rapid deployment. 1.IntroductionBiological agents are a significant threat to the national population, economy, and security (1, 2). Whether intentionally engineered or naturally occurring, biological threats including viruses, bacteria, and toxins require prepared response efforts (1, 3). The need for new vaccines against biological agents has driven interest in combining antigens from various pathogens into multi-pathogen vaccine platforms (4).Vaccines are important to overall biodefense as they serve to mitigate the impact of biological threats and to act as a deterrent (5). In the last 100 years, US troops have suffered more morbidity from infectious diseases than from combat (6). Biological threats to national security include risks to civilian populations, as demonstrated by the 2001 attacks where five people died after exposure to anthrax (7). Furthermore, since the 1990s, the threat of infectious diseases spreading in civilian populations from naturally occurring sources have been recognized as biosecurity threats (8). The pathogens and toxins that are most relevant to biodefense are defined disparately by different groups; here, we focus on pathogens listed by the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) as Category A-C “Bioterrorism agents” (9). While the focus of this review is on biodefense applications, vaccines against biological threat pathogens are also applicable in public health. For example, the recombinant vesicular stomatitis virus expressing Ebola (Zaire) glycoprotein (rVSV-ZEBOV) vaccine used extensively in Ebola virus disease outbreaks since 2015 was developed with funding from the Canadian Safety and Security Program (under the management of Defence Research and Development Canada) and the U.S. government (10). 2.Biological threat agentsBiological threat agents include pathogens and toxins capable of causing severe disease, high mortality, or substantial public-health disruption, particularly when they are highly virulent, readily transmissible, difficult to treat or prevent, or amenable to aerosol dissemination. Major biodefense families include filoviruses, arenaviruses, hantaviruses, flaviviruses, and bacterial and toxin agents. Filoviruses, including Ebola virus and Marburg virus cause severe hemorrhagic fever and exhibit limited cross-protection between genera and species, complicating vaccine development. Arenaviruses such as Lassa and Machupo viruses cause severe hemorrhagic disease, while their rodent reservoirs, broad geographic distribution, and limited vaccine availability increase their risk. Hantaviruses are rodent-associated and cause either severe hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome or hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, but are potential biological threats due to their ability to transmit via aerosol. Arboviruses, including flaviviruses and alphaviruses, can cause severe hemorrhagic or neurological disease and pose risks associated with widespread vector transmission and geographic distribution. Bacterial and toxin threats- including Bacillus anthracis, Yersinia pestis, Francisella tularensis, and botulinum neurotoxins- are characterized by high pathogenicity and, for several agents, the potential for aerosol dissemination. Collectively, these agents present biodefense challenges due to their virulence, diverse transmission routes, limited vaccine coverage or cross-protection, and potential for rapid or widespread dissemination. The ability to vaccinate people with a single formulation to provide protection against multiple diseases offers logistical advantages over single-pathogen vaccines in terms of resources and time. Another consideration is the speed of vaccine deployment, which can be attained by rapid large-scale production or long-term stockpiling (3). It is possible that a successful multi-pathogen formulation might make stockpiling of the vaccine for emergency use more appealing, as it provides coverage for several possible outbreaks instead of just one, making these considerations particularly relevant for biological threat agents, which are high mortality/morbidity pathogens with the potential to cause wide-spread outbreaks. 3.Protecting against multiple threats with a single formulationThe terminology used in multi-pathogen vaccination can be confusing and inconsistent across sources, and so this review will use the definitions from Lauer et al., 2017 (11).Multi-pathogen vaccines – Any vaccine formulation against multiple pathogens that is delivered in a single administration, including both combination vaccines and multivalent vaccines against two or more pathogens.Combination vaccines – A vaccine administered as a single formulation but composed of separate individual vaccines, like DTaP (diphtheria, tetanus, and acellular pertussis) vaccine. These are sometimes called cocktail vaccines.Multivalent vaccines – Single platform vaccines with multiple antigens designed to generate responses against antigens from distinct pathogens. This term is also used to describe single pathogen vaccines that use multiple antigens from the same pathogen.Vaccinating against multiple pathogens by combining individually successful vaccines typically results in robust responses to each vaccine. However, there are instances in which a given vaccine has lower efficacy when delivered in a cocktail or multi-pathogen formulation compared to when delivered separately, a phenomenon known as “vaccine interference” (12).Vaccine interference is a broad umbrella term, as lower efficacy of a vaccine when combined can result from multiple mechanisms of interference. The mechanisms of interference may not be apparent without testing specifically aimed at understanding the mechanism, increasing the numbers of controls and therefore the cost of experiments. Since testing vaccines in animal models prioritizes moving forward efficacious vaccine strategies over understanding poorly performing combinations, understanding why certain antigens can be combined successfully while others interfere requires extrapolation from known mechanisms, as well as understanding antigens, platform technologies and the animal models used in the vaccinations. This review will establish the known mechanisms of vaccine interference, discuss the existing literature on multi-pathogen vaccines in biodefense in the context of their different vaccine platforms and experimental conditions, and provide recommendations for predicting and testing interference in multi-pathogen vaccines. To highlight the phenomena, we will examine multi-pathogen vaccines that include the Marburg virus glycoprotein antigen, and discuss potential mechanisms of interference affecting this antigen. 4.Mechanisms of vaccine interferenceWhile there are well established examples of vaccines losing efficacy when combined, the underlying causes of the interference can be difficult to determine. There are multiple proposed mechanisms for how both combined and multivalent vaccines can interfere with one another. The proposed mechanisms can be grouped into three categories; epitope competition, immune response polarization and resource competition. full_text_sections.other: 1.IntroductionBiological agents are a significant threat to the national population, economy, and security (1, 2). Whether intentionally engineered or naturally occurring, biological threats including viruses, bacteria, and toxins require prepared response efforts (1, 3). The need for new vaccines against biological agents has driven interest in combining antigens from various pathogens into multi-pathogen vaccine platforms (4).Vaccines are important to overall biodefense as they serve to mitigate the impact of biological threats and to act as a deterrent (5). In the last 100 years, US troops have suffered more morbidity from infectious diseases than from combat (6). Biological threats to national security include risks to civilian populations, as demonstrated by the 2001 attacks where five people died after exposure to anthrax (7). Furthermore, since the 1990s, the threat of infectious diseases spreading in civilian populations from naturally occurring sources have been recognized as biosecurity threats (8). The pathogens and toxins that are most relevant to biodefense are defined disparately by different groups; here, we focus on pathogens listed by the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) as Category A-C “Bioterrorism agents” (9). While the focus of this review is on biodefense applications, vaccines against biological threat pathogens are also applicable in public health. For example, the recombinant vesicular stomatitis virus expressing Ebola (Zaire) glycoprotein (rVSV-ZEBOV) vaccine used extensively in Ebola virus disease outbreaks since 2015 was developed with funding from the Canadian Safety and Security Program (under the management of Defence Research and Development Canada) and the U.S. government (10). 2.Biological threat agentsBiological threat agents include pathogens and toxins capable of causing severe disease, high mortality, or substantial public-health disruption, particularly when they are highly virulent, readily transmissible, difficult to treat or prevent, or amenable to aerosol dissemination. Major biodefense families include filoviruses, arenaviruses, hantaviruses, flaviviruses, and bacterial and toxin agents. Filoviruses, including Ebola virus and Marburg virus cause severe hemorrhagic fever and exhibit limited cross-protection between genera and species, complicating vaccine development. Arenaviruses such as Lassa and Machupo viruses cause severe hemorrhagic disease, while their rodent reservoirs, broad geographic distribution, and limited vaccine availability increase their risk. Hantaviruses are rodent-associated and cause either severe hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome or hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, but are potential biological threats due to their ability to transmit via aerosol. Arboviruses, including flaviviruses and alphaviruses, can cause severe hemorrhagic or neurological disease and pose risks associated with widespread vector transmission and geographic distribution. Bacterial and toxin threats- including Bacillus anthracis, Yersinia pestis, Francisella tularensis, and botulinum neurotoxins- are characterized by high pathogenicity and, for several agents, the potential for aerosol dissemination. Collectively, these agents present biodefense challenges due to their virulence, diverse transmission routes, limited vaccine coverage or cross-protection, and potential for rapid or widespread dissemination. The ability to vaccinate people with a single formulation to provide protection against multiple diseases offers logistical advantages over single-pathogen vaccines in terms of resources and time. Another consideration is the speed of vaccine deployment, which can be attained by rapid large-scale production or long-term stockpiling (3). It is possible that a successful multi-pathogen formulation might make stockpiling of the vaccine for emergency use more appealing, as it provides coverage for several possible outbreaks instead of just one, making these considerations particularly relevant for biological threat agents, which are high mortality/morbidity pathogens with the potential to cause wide-spread outbreaks. 3.Protecting against multiple threats with a single formulationThe terminology used in multi-pathogen vaccination can be confusing and inconsistent across sources, and so this review will use the definitions from Lauer et al., 2017 (11).Multi-pathogen vaccines – Any vaccine formulation against multiple pathogens that is delivered in a single administration, including both combination vaccines and multivalent vaccines against two or more pathogens.Combination vaccines – A vaccine administered as a single formulation but composed of separate individual vaccines, like DTaP (diphtheria, tetanus, and acellular pertussis) vaccine. These are sometimes called cocktail vaccines.Multivalent vaccines – Single platform vaccines with multiple antigens designed to generate responses against antigens from distinct pathogens. This term is also used to describe single pathogen vaccines that use multiple antigens from the same pathogen.Vaccinating against multiple pathogens by combining individually successful vaccines typically results in robust responses to each vaccine. However, there are instances in which a given vaccine has lower efficacy when delivered in a cocktail or multi-pathogen formulation compared to when delivered separately, a phenomenon known as “vaccine interference” (12).Vaccine interference is a broad umbrella term, as lower efficacy of a vaccine when combined can result from multiple mechanisms of interference. The mechanisms of interference may not be apparent without testing specifically aimed at understanding the mechanism, increasing the numbers of controls and therefore the cost of experiments. Since testing vaccines in animal models prioritizes moving forward efficacious vaccine strategies over understanding poorly performing combinations, understanding why certain antigens can be combined successfully while others interfere requires extrapolation from known mechanisms, as well as understanding antigens, platform technologies and the animal models used in the vaccinations. analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to evaluate the development and evaluation of multi-pathogen vaccines for biological threat agents, particularly focusing on the challenges of vaccine interference and the need for standardized approaches to ensure effectiveness. The background highlighted the importance of multi-pathogen vaccines in biodefense due to their potential to protect against multiple diseases simultaneously.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study involved a comprehensive review of multi-pathogen vaccines for biodefense pathogens, including Marburg virus, and examined their development and evaluation strategies. It focused on vaccines targeting pathogens identified by the CDC bioterrorism agent list, with an emphasis on experimental designs and mechanisms of vaccine interference.
analysis.methods: The study conducted a systematic literature search using PubMed with specific vaccine and pathogen terms, including those related to Marburg virus. It manually filtered records to exclude those not relevant to multi-pathogen vaccines or the CDC bioterrorism agent list. Multiple reviewers were involved in the screening process to ensure consistency and reliability.
analysis.main_results: The study identified three core mechanisms of vaccine interference: epitope competition, resource competition, and immune polarization. analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted that multi-pathogen vaccines require careful experimental design to ensure they perform as effectively as their individual counterparts. analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings provide a critical framework for the development and evaluation of multi-pathogen vaccines, particularly for biodefense applications.
